title.narrative: Urban qualification in a key neighborhood of Belo Horizonte

description.narrative: Belo Horizonte, capital of the State of Minas Gerais, is in the Southeast region of Brazil, has a population of 2.5 million inhabitants. It is the main city of the third largest metropolitan region of the country, with a total of 5.9 million inhabitants. The municipal extension is of 331km² and is fully demarcated as an urban zone. Encouraged by the recent adoption of its new Master Plan in August 2019 (Law 11.181) — which is based most notably on the New Urban Agenda —, the municipality of Belo Horizonte wants to address the most challenging ‘informal’ urban expansion that is happening nowadays in the city (Region of Izidora). The region of Izidora corresponds to an area of about 9.5 km², in the northern vector of the city, next to the southern border of the city of Santa Luzia. This area is located in the largest green area of the city, counting around 280 water sources and 64 creeks, including part of the watershed that is Belo Horizonte’s main source of water. Part of Izidora has been squatted and is divided into four urban informal settlements - Esperança, Vitória, Helena Greco and Rosa Leão – totalizing approximately 1.5 km² and hosting about 4,200 precarious homes (which could be up to 7,000 families, given that there are no precise numbers since 2010), with families in situations of extreme poverty and without any available public infrastructure and relative services, as many Brazilian cities. During the Habitat III Conference in 2016, Izidora was highlighted as one of the most serious urban land conflicts in Latin America. Therefore, the new efforts of the municipality are a recognition of the issues, as well as the urgency of acting. In this sense, the squats were recently recognized as areas of social interest by the Municipality of Belo Horizonte through Decree No. 16.888, of April 12, 2018. The document indicates the need to further extend the comprehension and improvement of the region through studies on housing, environmental, urban and infrastructure conditions, as well as for the resolution of land conflicts – consequence of the squatting movement and the real estate interests.
